   And, perhaps, the remote prospect of a truly extreme solution: default.

   In August far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a candidate in next year’s presidential election, suggested canceling all the government debt held by the Bank of France, one of the national arms of the European Central Bank. “Throw it in the fire,” he said.

   (France’s national debt in August was 2.9 trillion euros, or $3.25 trillion, of which the Bank of France holds €544 billion.)

   Even if private creditors were spared, rating agencies might consider cancellation of central bank holdings a “selective default.” Partial repudiation could trigger payout on credit-default swaps.

   “Investors are no longer just debating France’s fiscal trajectory; they also have to consider the possibility that a future government might challenge the conventional treatment of some sovereign debt,” Gregory Peters, co-chief investment officer of PGIM Credit, told me. “My guess is the market is assigning this a low probability, but the consequences are large enough that it deserves some premium.”

   To be sure, polls put Mélenchon far behind Marine Le Pen of the National Rally, who just released a more orthodox plan to reduce the deficit. Cancellation would likely violate the treaties that govern French membership in the euro.

         The true significance of Mélenchon’s proposal is to reinforce in investors’ minds the unorthodox steps politicians around the world may take to deal with record debts while avoiding tough tax and spending decisions. President Trump has repeatedly called for the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates to make servicing the debt cheaper.

   Subordinating monetary policy to the Treasury is called “fiscal dominance” and usually leads to inflation. In an interview with Time last month, Trump suggested that might not be so bad: “Certain levels of inflation will also pay off that debt very rapidly.”

   Inflation, of course, reduces the real value of debt and is thus often labeled a form of soft default.

Despite a steep increase in tariffs, U.S. imports grew by 4.5% last year. The Dallas Fed estimates that imports would have declined by 12% had it not been for a surge in demand for computing equipment from overseas, as well as for companies’ efforts to front-run the tariffs. That trend has continued: Through August, imports were up another 4% over the same period last year, driven largely by tech hardware. Semiconductor imports are up 25%, computers 46% and computer accessories 52%.

   Post-MAGA economics . James M. Patterson writes that JD Vance has pledged to “thrust more daggers” into neoliberalism, favoring subsidies for U.S. manufacturers, reshoring supply chains, and de-emphasizing the dollar as a global reserve currency. Patterson sees a parallel with Spain’s experience under dictator Francisco Franco, whose record has won admiration from American “post-liberals” even though he abolished democracy. “Whatever problems one might have had with MAGA are nothing compared with what might replace it,” Patterson warns.

He assumes both will keep their current age-specific fertility and mortality rates and net immigration of zero. The result: Around 2128, China’s population, now 1.4 billion, will fall to 174 million while the U.S. population now 342 million, falls to just above 174 million.

         The Fed feels no urgency to raise interest rates   again, according to the September minutes published Wednesday. Most policymakers see at least one more increase. But the minutes merely said that most of the committee expected another hike before the end of the year , a framing aligned with key Fed officials who have downplayed an October hike. Jon Hilsenrath, a former WSJ Fed reporter who now runs Serpa Pinto Advisory, notes that under Chairman Kevin Warsh, the minutes have continued to shrink and lose detail.

   • France is considering borrowing more money short term as it faces a financial reckoning over runaway spending.

       What to Watch   Friday 

   • Economists expect the University of Michigan’s preliminary October consumer-sentiment result to decline a tick to 48, from 48.1 in the final September reading.

   • At noon I’ll join Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick to discuss their book, The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There , on a panel hosted by the American Enterprise Institute. Register to watch here . 

   Monday 

   • The bond market is closed for Columbus Day, but the stock market is open.

       What I’m Reading   • Amid the Iran war, the cost of hiring a tanker to move U.S. oil to Asia is up 740% from last year’s average price. ( Bloomberg )

Default May Be the Tail Risk Haunting French Bonds
 
Plus, a growing trade deficit, MAGA economics after Trump, and the Fed’s rate-hike outlook
 

The spike in French bond yields is mostly driven by the country’s crushing debt and politicians’ inability to agree on a solution.

 

And, perhaps, the remote prospect of a truly extreme solution: default.

 

In August far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a candidate in next year’s presidential election, suggested canceling all the government debt held by the Bank of France, one of the national arms of the European Central Bank. “Throw it in the fire,” he said.

 

(France’s national debt in August was 2.9 trillion euros, or $3.25 trillion, of which the Bank of France holds €544 billion.)

 

Even if private creditors were spared, rating agencies might consider cancellation of central bank holdings a “selective default.” Partial repudiation could trigger payout on credit-default swaps.

 

“Investors are no longer just debating France’s fiscal trajectory; they also have to consider the possibility that a future government might challenge the conventional treatment of some sovereign debt,” Gregory Peters, co-chief investment officer of PGIM Credit, told me. “My guess is the market is assigning this a low probability, but the consequences are large enough that it deserves some premium.”

 

To be sure, polls put Mélenchon far behind Marine Le Pen of the National Rally, who just released a more orthodox plan to reduce the deficit. Cancellation would likely violate the treaties that govern French membership in the euro.

 
 
 
 

The true significance of Mélenchon’s proposal is to reinforce in investors’ minds the unorthodox steps politicians around the world may take to deal with record debts while avoiding tough tax and spending decisions. President Trump has repeatedly called for the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates to make servicing the debt cheaper.

 

Subordinating monetary policy to the Treasury is called “fiscal dominance” and usually leads to inflation. In an interview with Time last month, Trump suggested that might not be so bad: “Certain levels of inflation will also pay off that debt very rapidly.”

 

Inflation, of course, reduces the real value of debt and is thus often labeled a form of soft default.

What I’m Following

 

The AI investment boom is frustrating Trump’s ambition to shrink the trade deficit. Despite a steep increase in tariffs, U.S. imports grew by 4.5% last year. The Dallas Fed estimates that imports would have declined by 12% had it not been for a surge in demand for computing equipment from overseas, as well as for companies’ efforts to front-run the tariffs. That trend has continued: Through August, imports were up another 4% over the same period last year, driven largely by tech hardware. Semiconductor imports are up 25%, computers 46% and computer accessories 52%.

 

Post-MAGA economics. James M. Patterson writes that JD Vance has pledged to “thrust more daggers” into neoliberalism, favoring subsidies for U.S. manufacturers, reshoring supply chains, and de-emphasizing the dollar as a global reserve currency. Patterson sees a parallel with Spain’s experience under dictator Francisco Franco, whose record has won admiration from American “post-liberals” even though he abolished democracy. “Whatever problems one might have had with MAGA are nothing compared with what might replace it,” Patterson warns.

 

China’s population will fall below the U.S.’s in about a century, Jesús Fernandez-Villaverde of the University of Pennsylvania, who specializes in demographics, calculates. He assumes both will keep their current age-specific fertility and mortality rates and net immigration of zero. The result: Around 2128, China’s population, now 1.4 billion, will fall to 174 million while the U.S. population now 342 million, falls to just above 174 million.

 
 
 
 

The Fed feels no urgency to raise interest rates again, according to the September minutes published Wednesday. Most policymakers see at least one more increase. But the minutes merely said that most of the committee expected another hike before the end of the year, a framing aligned with key Fed officials who have downplayed an October hike. Jon Hilsenrath, a former WSJ Fed reporter who now runs Serpa Pinto Advisory, notes that under Chairman Kevin Warsh, the minutes have continued to shrink and lose detail.

CHIP SOMODEVILLA/GETTY IMAGES
 

• As Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent often loses his temper and excoriates staff while progress on the administration’s key economic goals has slipped. Yet he has stayed in Trump’s good graces and consolidated power.

 

• Relations are cooling between the Trump administration and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum over drug-enforcement sanctions. “Let’s be clear: First they come for some, then for others, until offices of the Department of Justice decide elections in Mexico,” Sheinbaum said at a rally earlier this year.

 

• France is considering borrowing more money short term as it faces a financial reckoning over runaway spending.
